overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Logic Behind the Eighteen Decrees
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 14a–14b
overview.hebrewSource: מַתָּנָה טוֹבָה יֵשׁ לִי בְּבֵית גְּנָזַי
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Having listed the eighteen decrees issued in Ḥananya ben Ḥizkiya's attic, the Gemara now works through the reason behind each one: why eating or drinking impure items disqualifies teruma, why drawn water after immersion is a problem, why a Torah scroll and unwashed hands were singled out. It then asks a historical question — were these decrees, especially the one on hands, issued by Hillel and Shammai themselves or only by their students? — and traces the decree back even further, to King Solomon's own institution of hand-washing and eiruvin.

slides.title: 🤔 The Reasons Behind the Decrees
slides.subtitle: Each concern traces back to protecting teruma from contamination
rows: Eating first- or second-degree impure food disqualifies teruma
Lest he then drink teruma liquid and disqualify it with impurity still in his mouth
Lest he then eat teruma food with an impure mouth — a separate decree, since eating after drinking is less common than drinking after eating
Head/majority of body entering drawn water after immersion
People used to rinse foul cave water off themselves with drawn water, then began saying the drawn water itself — not only the cave water — was what purified them
A pure person on whom three log of drawn water fell
Needed so people could distinguish someone freshly immersed from someone who was never impure at all

slides.title: 📜 Mice, Teruma, and a Torah Scroll
slides.subtitle: Rav Mesharshiya explains the decree on scrolls
slides.label: The reasoning:
slides.text: Priests used to store teruma foods beside a Torah scroll, reasoning: 'this is holy, and that is holy' — fitting company for one another. But mice drawn to the food would gnaw at the scrolls as well. Once the Sages saw the scrolls coming to ruin, they decreed that contact with a Torah scroll disqualifies teruma — so that priests would stop storing the two together, protecting the scrolls.

nodes.content: ❓ Why did the Sages decree impurity specifically on unwashed hands?
💡 'Hands are busy' (עַסְקָנִיּוֹת) — they touch things constantly without one paying attention
📜 Baraita: even hands that became impure by touching a Torah scroll disqualify teruma

columns.label: R' Parnakh / R' Yoḥanan
columns.content: One who holds an uncovered Torah scroll is 'buried naked'

columns.label: Rabbi Zeira, refined twice
columns.content: Not literally naked — 'naked of mitzvot'; refined again: he loses credit only for that one mitzva, for handling the scroll improperly

slides.title: 📚 Whose Decree Was It — the Masters, or Their Students?
slides.subtitle: Reconciling a baraita with Shmuel's count of the disputes

steps.content: 1️⃣ Baraita: Yosei ben Yo'ezer and Yosei ben Yoḥanan decreed impurity on the land of the nations and glass vessels; Shimon ben Shataḥ decreed on metal vessels; Shammai and Hillel themselves decreed on hands

2️⃣ Problem: Shmuel taught that all eighteen decrees, hands included, were disputed only among Shammai's and Hillel's students in the attic — while Hillel and Shammai personally disagreed in just three places
3️⃣ Resolution: Hillel and Shammai themselves came and decreed on hands, but the people did not accept it from them; their students later came, decreed again, and this time the people accepted it
4️⃣ Ilfa: from the very beginning, the decree on hands was that contact renders teruma fit for burning — unlike other decrees, which began merely 'in abeyance'

slides.title: 👑 An Even Earlier Decree — King Solomon
slides.subtitle: Pushing the question of hand-impurity back further still

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: Still unclear — didn't Solomon already decree the washing of hands, alongside eiruvin, long before Hillel and Shammai?

lines.speaker: Rav Yehuda
lines.text: quoting Shmuel: when Solomon instituted eiruvin and the washing of hands, a Divine Voice went out and declared: 'My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will rejoice, even mine' (Proverbs 23:15).

callout.label: To be continued:
callout.text: The Gemara's answer carries onto the next amud, distinguishing what Solomon's decree covered from what Hillel, Shammai, and their students later added.

summary.principle: Each of the eighteen decrees traces back to a concrete, practical concern — protecting teruma from careless hands, wandering mice, or drawn water mistaken for purifying water — and even the famous decree on hands turns out to have a layered history reaching back to Solomon.

flowSteps.content: 🤔 Each decree guards teruma: impure food or drink in the mouth, drawn water misunderstood as purifying
📜 Storing teruma beside a Torah scroll drew mice — so contact with a scroll now disqualifies teruma

columns.content: ✋ 'Busy hands' are decreed impure; mishandling a scroll costs credit for that mitzva alone
📚 Shammai and Hillel decreed on hands first, but only their students' repeat decree was accepted

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Even Solomon had already instituted washing of hands and eiruvin — the decrees here build on, and extend, layers of earlier practice

quiz.q: Why did the Sages decree that one who eats first- or second-degree impure food disqualifies teruma?
o: Because such food is always visibly rotten
Lest he then drink teruma liquid and disqualify it with impurity still in his mouth
Because eating impure food is itself a Torah-level prohibition
To discourage eating between meals
quiz.e: The concern is practical: after eating impure food, he might drink teruma liquid and thereby disqualify it via his mouth.

quiz.q: Why, according to Rav Mesharshiya, did storing teruma beside a Torah scroll lead to a decree of impurity on the scroll?
o: Because teruma itself is holier than a Torah scroll
Because mice, drawn to the stored food, would gnaw at the scrolls as well
Because it violated the honor of the scroll to be touched
Because priests could no longer find their scrolls
quiz.e: Priests stored teruma next to scrolls reasoning 'this is holy and that is holy,' but the food attracted mice that damaged the scrolls, prompting the Sages to decree impurity on scrolls to stop the practice.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Zeira's refined understanding, what does it mean that one who holds an uncovered Torah scroll is 'buried naked'?
o: He is literally buried without clothing
He loses credit for all the mitzvot he ever performed
He loses credit specifically for that one mitzva, having performed it improperly
He is barred from burial in a Jewish cemetery
quiz.e: Rabbi Zeira refined the statement twice, ultimately explaining that the person forfeits credit only for that particular mitzva — handling the scroll — not all his merits.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara reconcile the baraita crediting Shammai and Hillel themselves with decreeing on hands, against Shmuel's statement that all eighteen decrees were disputed only by their students?
o: The baraita is simply mistaken and rejected
Shammai and Hillel decreed first but the people did not accept it from them; their students later decreed again and it was accepted
Shammai and Hillel only discussed hands theoretically, without issuing a decree
Shmuel's statement refers to a different set of decrees entirely
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that Shammai and Hillel's original decree on hands was not accepted by the people; only when their students repeated the decree was it accepted, aligning with Shmuel's count of the students' disputes.

quiz.q: According to Ilfa, what was distinctive about the decree of impurity on hands from its very inception?
o: It applied only to priests
Unlike other decrees, which began merely 'in abeyance,' the hand decree from the start rendered teruma fit for burning
It was the very first of the eighteen decrees enacted
It required a public vote before taking effect
quiz.e: Ilfa taught that, unlike decrees that started as a lesser status of doubt ('in abeyance'), the decree on hands was severe from the outset, requiring that teruma touched by impure hands be burned.
